corrected_draft.title: DHS Announces Termination of Afghanistan TPS Designation
corrected_draft.description_short: DHS announced in May 2025 that Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation would end effective July 14, 2025; Ukraine’s TPS was extended earlier that year.
corrected_draft.description_medium: A May 2025 Federal Register notice announced DHS’s termination of Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, effective July 14, 2025. The notice addressed Afghanistan specifically. Separately, DHS announced in January 2025 an 18-month extension of Ukraine TPS through October 19, 2026. These were separate country-specific actions, not a March termination of TPS for millions of refugees from Afghanistan, Ukraine and other countries.
corrected_draft.description_long: In a Federal Register notice published in May 2025, the Department of Homeland Security announced the termination of Afghanistan’s Temporary Protected Status designation, with termination effective July 14, 2025. The notice describes Afghanistan’s earlier TPS designation and extension and explains the Secretary’s review and determination. It concerns Afghanistan and does not describe a simultaneous termination for Ukrainians, Venezuelans, Haitians, Salvadorans and other nationalities. In a separate January 2025 notice, DHS extended Ukraine’s TPS designation for 18 months, through October 19, 2026, and permitted current beneficiaries to re-register. These distinct government actions contradict the title’s combined claim that Afghanistan and Ukraine TPS were both ended as part of a March action. A corrected entry can record the later Afghanistan termination as its own discrete event, with its actual announcement and effective dates. It should not claim that all TPS protections for millions ended together.

corrected_draft.title: Trump Calls MS-13 Members “Animals” at California Roundtable
corrected_draft.description_short: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable on California sanctuary policies, Trump said “These are animals” immediately after discussing MS-13 gang members.
corrected_draft.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable about California sanctuary policies, President Donald Trump discussed MS-13 gang members and said, “These are animals.” The archived White House transcript places the phrase directly after his reference to MS-13. This supports a precisely contextualized account of the remark; it does not support the entry’s framing that he called immigrants generally “animals” at a California roundtable in 2025.
corrected_draft.description_long: At a May 16, 2018 White House roundtable on California sanctuary policies, President Donald Trump discussed immigration enforcement and MS-13 gang members. In the archived transcript, Trump referred to MS-13 immediately before saying, “These are animals.” The transcript therefore supports that he used the word during the roundtable, in a passage specifically discussing the gang. It does not establish that the phrase described immigrants generally, and it does not place the remark at a July 2019 Cincinnati rally. The transcript records that Sheriff Margaret Mims first described a possible MS-13 member she could not report to ICE under a local threshold, then Trump replied about people entering the country and said, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” The setting was a roundtable on California sanctuary policies. The transcript supports the statement and its immediate discussion; it does not resolve every later dispute over how broadly Trump meant it.

corrected_draft.title: State Department Orders Social Media Vetting for Visa Applicants Who Have Been to Gaza
corrected_draft.description_short: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered social-media vetting for visa applicants who had been in Gaza on or after January 1, 2007.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On April 17, 2025, the State Department directed U.S. diplomatic missions to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in Gaza since January 1, 2007. Reuters reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed the cable. This is a narrower and better-supported event than the entry’s claim that DHS revoked visas simply for posts critical of Israel; the cable concerned screening and security review, not a blanket automatic revocation rule.
corrected_draft.description_long: On April 17, 2025, the State Department ordered U.S. diplomatic and consular posts to conduct social-media vetting for immigrant and nonimmigrant visa applicants who had been in the Gaza Strip on or after January 1, 2007. Reuters reported the directive from an internal cable signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The cable instructed that potentially derogatory security information found in an online review should prompt a security advisory opinion. Reuters also reported that the administration had revoked hundreds of visas in other cases and that officials had cited foreign-policy concerns involving some student visa holders. Those broader actions do not show that DHS revoked visas across the board because applicants had posted criticism of Israel. The corrected entry should identify the State Department’s Gaza-related screening directive, preserve its applicant scope and date, and avoid merging it with separate visa-revocation cases or attributing it to DHS.
